new_statements.quote: 3. SYLLABLE STRESS Primary syllable stress occurs on the first syllable of each word. In three syllable words there is decreasing stress after the first syllable. In reduplicated forms there is equal stress on the first syllable of each reduplicated stem. In compounded words there is primary stress on the first syllable of the first member and secondary stress on the first syllable of the second member of the compound. Other polysyllables take secondary stess [sic] on the penultimate syllable. Stress is therefore predictable and non-phonemic, and will not be symbolized in the phonemic [transcription]. [Elsewhere in the 1968 edn:] Accent (primary syllable stress) falls on the first syllable of each native word having more than one syllable

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable) (initial primary; for four-syllable words secondary on the penult = syllable 3 gives 1010). Refines it: secondary stress is stated as penultimate for all longer polysyllables (a five-syllable word would be 10010, not alternating), separate rules for compounds and reduplications, and an explicit non-phonemic statement. The text was read only through Open Library search-inside snippets, since both archive.org items are lending-restricted ( not reachable by automated download, item search 'Item not available'); the snippets overlap end-to-end so the section is continuous.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of every word; stress is predictable and non-phonemic. Three-syllable words: stress decreasing after the first syllable. Longer non-compound polysyllables: secondary stress on the penultimate syllable. Compounds: primary on the first syllable of the first member, secondary on the first syllable of the second member. Reduplications: equal stress on the first syllable of each stem.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Penultimate syllable in polysyllables of more than three syllables; first syllable of the second member in compounds; equal stress on each stem in reduplications (e.g. pinta-pinta 'moth', kutjal-kutjal 'four').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; compounds and reduplications are treated separately as above.
new_statements.identity_note: Douglas 1968/1976 describes the 'Njuŋar' (Nyungar) speech of the South-West as spoken in the 1960s-70s (the koine of the old dialects), which is the catalog's Nyunga (Noongar) nyun1247 and also the StressTyp2 entry for this language 'Juat' (its example words pinta-pinta 'moth' and pininjku 'generation level' are Douglas's). Thieberger's handbook statement is regional: it covers every language south of the Kimberley and names Nyungar only for the extra vowel letters e and o. Smith-Ali et al. 2023 (Noongar, modern community orthography) and Dench 1994 were not readable.

new_statements.quote: And for Nyungar languages the following letters are needed: e as in pet, o as in pot. Word stress is usually on the first syllable, so it is the first part of the word that sounds the loudest. For example, in the English word 'radio', stress occurs on the first part of the word 'radio', in 'retire' stress occurs in the second part of the word.
